blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 21 (Halogenoalkanes), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 What are halogenoalkanes? Explain their classification (i) on the basis of the number of halogen atoms (ii) monohalogenoalkanes into primary, secondary and tertiary, with examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A halogenoalkane is formed when one or more hydrogen atoms of an alkane are replaced by halogen atoms.

(i) Number of halogen atoms (–X): mono-, di-, tri- or polyhalogenoalkanes, e.g. CH₃X (mono), CH₂X₂ (di), CHX₃ (tri).
Monohalogenoalkanes are also called alkyl halides, general formula R – X (R = methyl, ethyl, propyl, etc.; X = F, Cl, Br, I).

(ii) Type of carbon bearing the halogen:
• Primary: the halogen-bearing carbon is attached to one or no carbon atom, e.g. CH₃–Cl (chloromethane), CH₃–CH₂–Cl (chloroethane), CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–Cl (1-chloropropane).
• Secondary: the halogen-bearing carbon is directly attached to two other carbon atoms, e.g. CH₃–CHCl–CH₃ (2-chloropropane), CH₃–CHCl–CH₂–CH₃ (2-chlorobutane).
• Tertiary: the halogen-bearing carbon is directly attached to three carbon atoms, e.g. (CH₃)₃C–Cl (2-chloro-2-methylpropane).

book_ref.quote: A halogenoalkane is formed when one or more hydrogen atoms of an alkane are replaced by halogen atoms

blocks.prompt: 2 Describe the uses of halogenoalkanes in daily life. Explain the use of halothane and what is replacing CFCs. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Halogenoalkanes are very useful in daily life, mainly due to their specialized chemical stability.
• Refrigerants and propellants: chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) were used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants. They are being replaced by hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), which contain no chlorine. (Freons are themselves CFCs, e.g. Freon-12 is CCl₂F₂, so they are not the replacement.)
• Medicine: halogenated compounds are powerful anesthetics. Halothane, CF₃–CHClBr, is a powerful inhalation anesthetic that induces a reversible loss of consciousness during surgeries. Chloroform and other chlorinated anesthetics used earlier are now banned due to their toxicity and safety concerns.
• Polymers: they are vital intermediates for PVC (polyvinyl chloride) for piping and PTFE (Teflon) for non-stick cookware.

book_ref.quote: Halogenoalkanes are very useful in daily life, primarily due to their specialized chemical stability

blocks.prompt: 3 Describe the preparation of halogenoalkanes from (i) an alkane (ii) an alkene (iii) an alcohol with a halogen acid (iv) an alcohol with PBr₃. Give one equation for each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) From an alkane: halogenation in the presence of light.
CH₃–CH₃ + Cl₂ —(light)→ CH₃–CH₂–Cl + HCl

(ii) From an alkene: electrophilic addition of a hydrogen halide.
H₂C=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃–CH₂–Br

(iii) From an alcohol with a halogen acid, ZnCl₂ acting as a catalyst.
CH₃–CH₂–OH + HCl —(ZnCl₂)→ CH₃–CH₂–Cl + H₂O

(iv) From an alcohol with a phosphorus trihalide, which replaces the –OH group by a halo group.
3CH₃–CH₂–OH + PBr₃ → 3CH₃–CH₂–Br + H₃PO₃

book_ref.quote: Halogenoalkanes can be prepared by the halogenation of alkanes in the presence of light

blocks.prompt: 4 Explain, with equations, the special advantage of (i) the thionyl chloride method for chloroalkanes (ii) the potassium bromide–acid method, and why phosphoric acid is preferred for iodoalkanes. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Thionyl chloride method: alcohols react with SOCl₂ with pyridine as a catalyst.
CH₃–CH₂–OH + SOCl₂ —(pyridine)→ CH₃–CH₂–Cl + SO₂ + HCl
It is especially useful because the by-products, SO₂ and HCl, are gases which go off, leaving behind the pure product.

(ii) KBr–acid method: the alcohol is heated with KBr and an acid such as H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄. The acid first reacts with KBr to give HBr, which then converts the alcohol into the bromoalkane.
CH₃–CH₂–OH + KBr + H₂SO₄ → CH₃–CH₂–Br + H₂O + KHSO₄
This method is commonly used to prepare bromoalkanes and iodoalkanes.

Phosphoric acid for iodoalkanes: H₃PO₄ is a weak oxidizing agent and is less likely to oxidize iodide ions to iodine, so the iodide stays available to form the iodoalkane.

book_ref.quote: Phosphoric acid is preferably used to prepare iodoalkanes because it is a weak oxidizing agent

blocks.prompt: 5 Discuss the reactivity of halogenoalkanes in terms of the carbon–halogen bond energies. Give the order of reactivity and other factors that affect it. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A halogenoalkane R – X has an alkyl group with a partial positive charge on the carbon attached to the halogen, and the halogen with a partial negative charge. Experiments show that the strength of the C – X bond is the main factor deciding reactivity: the weaker bond is broken more easily and makes the molecule more reactive.

Bond energies (Table 21.1) are given in the table below.

Iodo compounds have the weakest bonds and are the most reactive; fluoro compounds are the least reactive:
R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F
The C – F bond is so strong that fluoroalkanes do not react under ordinary conditions.

Other factors that may affect reactivity: bond polarity, steric hindrance and inductive effect.

book_ref.quote: Experiments have shown that the strength of carbon halogen bond is the main factor

blocks.prompt: 6 Explain why halogenoalkanes undergo nucleophilic substitution and elimination reactions. Write the general equation of each, labelling the species. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The C–X bond is polar because of the difference of electronegativity between carbon and the halogen. Two kinds of attack are therefore possible:

(a) Nucleophilic substitution (SN): the δ+ carbon is an electrophilic centre and is attacked by a nucleophile; the halogen is replaced by another atom or group.
Nu⁻ + R–X → R–Nu + X⁻
(attacking nucleophile + substrate molecule → substituted product + leaving group)

(b) Elimination (E): a base attacks the hydrogen on the carbon next to the C–X carbon; HX is removed and an alkene forms.
H–C–C–X (substrate) → C=C (alkene) + HX (hydrogen halide)

The two reactions take place under similar conditions and often compete with each other.

book_ref.quote: These two possibilities result in two types of reaction of halogenoalkanes

blocks.prompt: 7 Describe the SN2 mechanism using the reaction of bromomethane with hydroxide ion. Discuss its molecularity and kinetics, and explain why primary halogenoalkanes follow it. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
SN2 (nucleophilic substitution bimolecular) is a single-step mechanism.

Mechanism: OH⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon of CH₃–Br from the side opposite to the leaving group (Br). As soon as the nucleophile starts attacking, the C–Br bond starts breaking; the extent of bond formation equals the extent of bond breaking. A transition state [HO---CH₃---Br]⁻ is passed, and the products are formed:
OH⁻ + CH₃–Br → [HO---CH₃---Br]⁻ → CH₃–OH + Br⁻

Molecularity: the one step is the rate-determining step and two molecules take part in it, so it is bimolecular.

Kinetics: the rate depends on both the alkyl halide and the nucleophile:
Rate = k[alkyl halide]¹[nucleophile]¹, order = 1 + 1 = 2 (second order).

Primary halides: for steric reasons; the substrate carbon carries hydrogen atoms or only one carbon atom, so the nucleophile can approach and attack it easily from the back. Primary monohalogenoalkanes always follow SN2.

book_ref.quote: This is a single step mechanism

blocks.prompt: 8 Describe the SN1 mechanism taking 2-bromo-2-methylpropane and hydroxide ion as an example. Explain its rate equation and why tertiary halogenoalkanes follow this mechanism. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
SN1 (nucleophilic substitution unimolecular) involves two steps.

Step 1 (slow): reversible ionization of the alkyl halide in aqueous acetone or aqueous ethyl alcohol gives a carbocation intermediate.
(CH₃)₃C–Br ⇌ (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻
Step 2 (fast): the carbocation is attacked by the nucleophile.
(CH₃)₃C⁺ + OH⁻ → (CH₃)₃C–OH

Step 1 breaks a covalent bond, so it is slow compared with step 2 (an energetically favourable combination of ions); it is the rate-determining step. Only one molecule takes part in it, so the mechanism is unimolecular and first order:
Rate = k[alkyl halide]

Tertiary halides always follow SN1 because (i) they form a stable tertiary carbocation, and (ii) three bulky groups on the electrophilic carbon prevent the nucleophile from attacking from the backside of the leaving group.

book_ref.quote: This type of mechanism involves two steps

blocks.prompt: 9 What is a carbocation? Explain the order of stability of carbocations and its importance in deciding the mechanism followed by primary, secondary and tertiary halogenoalkanes. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A carbocation is the positively charged carbon intermediate formed when the C–X bond of an alkyl halide ionizes in the first step of SN1 (and E1).

Order of stability:
tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl carbocation
Alkyl (CH₃) groups push electrons towards the positive carbon (positive inductive effect, +I). A tertiary carbocation has three such groups, a secondary two, a primary one and the methyl carbocation none; as the +I effect decreases, stability decreases.

Importance: the carbocation is formed in the rate-determining step, so the more stable the carbocation, the more easily it is formed.
• Tertiary halides form the stable 3° carbocation (and hinder backside attack): SN1.
• Primary halides would give an unstable carbocation but are open to backside attack: SN2.
• Secondary halides can follow both SN2 and SN1, depending upon the nature of the solvent.

book_ref.quote: The mechanism shows that a carbocation is formed in the rate-determining step

blocks.prompt: 10 Bromoethane reacts with OH⁻ by the SN2 mechanism with k = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹. Calculate (i) the rate when [bromoethane] = 0.25 mol dm⁻³ and [OH⁻] = 0.15 mol dm⁻³ (ii) the rate when [OH⁻] is doubled at the same [bromoethane]. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: SN2 is second order, Rate = k[alkyl halide][nucleophile]; put in the values, then note the rate is directly proportional to [OH⁻].

book_ref.quote: Kinetic studies of the reactions involving SN2 mechanism have shown

steps: Rate equation for SN2: Rate = k[CH₃CH₂Br][OH⁻]
Rate = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.25 × 0.30 = 2.25 × 10⁻⁵ ≈ 2.3 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (twice the rate in (i))
blocks.final_answer: (i) 1.1 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (ii) 2.3 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹; the rate doubles.

blocks.prompt: 12 What is β-elimination? Describe the E2 mechanism using bromoethane, and give its molecularity and rate equation. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
β-Elimination: a reaction in which a hydrogen atom on the β-carbon of the alkyl halide and the halogen atom on the adjacent carbon are removed, when a base attacks the β-hydrogen. An alkene is obtained instead of a substitution product. These reactions take place along with substitution reactions and often compete with them; they follow E2 or E1.

E2 mechanism (single step): the base attacks a β-hydrogen and the leaving group leaves at the same time, with the formation of a C=C bond. For bromoethane the base takes an H from CH₃, the C–H electrons form the C=C bond and Br leaves as Br⁻:
Base⁻ + H–CH₂–CH₂–Br → CH₂=CH₂ + H–Base + Br⁻

Molecularity: two (bimolecular), like SN2.
Rate = k[alkyl halide]¹[base]¹, order = 1 + 1 = 2 (second order).
Primary halogenoalkanes generally follow E2.

blocks.prompt: 13 Describe the E1 mechanism using 2-bromo-2-methylpropane. Which halogenoalkanes follow E1, E2 or both? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
E1 (elimination unimolecular) has two steps.

Step 1 (slow): like SN1, the substrate ionizes to give a carbocation.
(CH₃)₃C–Br ⇌ (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻ (3° carbocation)
Step 2 (fast): the base attacks a β-hydrogen; the C–H electrons form the C=C bond.
(CH₃)₃C⁺ + Base⁻ → (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ (2-methylpropene) + H–Base

Only the alkyl halide takes part in the slow step, so E1 is unimolecular; its rate depends only on the concentration of the alkyl halide: Rate = k[alkyl halide].

Which substrates: primary halogenoalkanes generally follow E2, tertiary follow E1, and secondary can show both E2 and E1 according to the choice of the solvent.

book_ref.quote: E1 mechanism is a unimolecular mechanism

blocks.prompt: 14 Bromoethane undergoes E2 elimination with a base, k = 5.0 × 10⁻³ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹. Calculate (i) the rate when [bromoethane] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³ and [base] = 0.50 mol dm⁻³ (ii) the rate when [bromoethane] is tripled and [base] is halved. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: E2 is second order, Rate = k[alkyl halide][base]; both concentrations change the rate.

book_ref.quote: Like SN2 reactions, the molecularity of E2 reactions is also two

steps: Rate equation for E2: Rate = k[CH₃CH₂Br][base]
blocks.final_answer: (i) 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (ii) 3.8 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (1.5 times)

blocks.prompt: 15 Explain how sodium hydroxide gives both substitution and elimination products with bromoethane. Write both equations and state the conditions. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A halogenoalkane reacts with sodium hydroxide to give both substitution and elimination products, depending on the conditions, because the hydroxide ion is both a good nucleophile and a good base.

As a nucleophile, OH⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon and replaces the halogen, giving an alcohol (substitution). With aqueous NaOH:
CH₃–CH₂–Br + NaOH —(aqueous)→ CH₃–CH₂–OH + NaBr

As a base, OH⁻ removes the β-hydrogen, and the halogen leaves, giving an alkene (elimination). With NaOH in alcohol:
CH₃–CH₂–Br + NaOH —(alcohol)→ CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O + NaBr

Conditions: the reactions take place at a higher temperature under reflux, to avoid the loss of the volatile products.

book_ref.quote: Hydroxide ion is both a good nucleophile and a good base

blocks.prompt: 16 Describe the step-by-step reaction of ammonia with bromoethane up to the quaternary ammonium salt. Why is a mixture of products obtained? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Ammonia is a good nucleophile; the lone pair on N attacks the δ+ carbon of bromoethane and Br leaves.

Step 1: NH₃ + C₂H₅Br → C₂H₅NH₂ (ethanamine) + HBr
Step 2: ethanamine is also a nucleophile and competes with ammonia:
C₂H₅NH₂ + C₂H₅Br → (C₂H₅)₂NH (N-ethylethanamine, diethyl amine) + HBr
Step 3: N-ethylethanamine attacks another bromoethane:
(C₂H₅)₂NH + C₂H₅Br → (C₂H₅)₃N (N,N-diethylethanamine) + HBr
Step 4: with a large excess of bromoethane, a quaternary ammonium salt forms:
(C₂H₅)₃N + C₂H₅Br → [(C₂H₅)₄N]⁺ Br⁻ (N,N,N-triethylethanaminium bromide)

Mixture: each amine formed still has a lone pair and is a nucleophile, so it reacts further. Different amines are obtained by carefully controlling the amounts of halogenoalkane and ammonia.

book_ref.quote: Different types of amines can be produced if the amounts of halogenoalkane and ammonia are carefully controlled

blocks.prompt: 17 Describe the reaction of halogenoalkanes with aqueous silver nitrate. How does it help to identify the halogen and compare the reactivities of halogenoalkanes? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The reaction is carried out in a mixture of water and ethanol; the ethanol helps to dissolve the halogenoalkane. Water acts as a nucleophile and replaces the halide ion:
CH₃–CH₂–X + H–OH → CH₃–CH₂–OH + H⁺ + X⁻

Identification: the released halide ion reacts with silver nitrate to give a precipitate with a characteristic colour:
Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl (white ppt)
Ag⁺ + Br⁻ → AgBr (cream yellow ppt)
Ag⁺ + I⁻ → AgI (bright yellow ppt)

Reactivity: the quicker the precipitate appears, the more reactive the halogenoalkane. An iodoalkane gives a precipitate much quicker than a bromoalkane, while a chloroalkane reacts very slowly. This agrees with the C–X bond energies (C–I weakest): R–I > R–Br > R–Cl.

book_ref.quote: Comparing the rates of formation of silver halides in this reaction gives us a clue

blocks.prompt: 18 How are halogenoarenes prepared? Explain, with the help of delocalisation, why chlorobenzene is less reactive than a halogenoalkane towards nucleophiles. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Preparation: chlorobenzene and bromobenzene are prepared by reacting benzene with chlorine or bromine in the presence of a catalyst, anhydrous FeCl₃ or FeBr₃, at room temperature. The reaction is an electrophilic aromatic substitution:
C₆H₆ + Cl₂ —(FeCl₃)→ C₆H₅Cl + HCl
C₆H₆ + Br₂ —(FeBr₃)→ C₆H₅Br + HBr

Lower reactivity: in a halogenoalkane the δ+ carbon of the C–X bond invites nucleophiles, giving substitution (and bases give elimination). In chlorobenzene, a lone pair on the chlorine atom is delocalised into the aromatic ring. This gives the C—Cl bond partial double-bond character, so it becomes stronger and difficult to break. Consequently halogenoarenes are less reactive and synthetically less useful.

book_ref.quote: Halogenoarenes like chlorobenzene and bromobenzene are prepared by reacting benzene
